subsection: 3. Gender socialisation and its impact on participation

notes.b: Gender socialisation shapes which activities young people see as open to them.
points: Socialisation: the lifelong process of learning the norms, values and behaviour expected in a society.
Gender socialisation: learning what is seen as appropriate for boys and men, and for girls and women.
Family: the toys children are given, the activities encouraged and the behaviour praised.
Peers: friends reward behaviour that fits gender norms and mock behaviour that does not.
School: the activities offered and the expectations teachers hold.
Media: the images of male and female athletes that young people see.
Sports clubs and coaches: the activities offered and the language used with boys and girls.
Religion and culture: the roles and behaviour a community treats as proper for each sex.

notes.h: Examples of gender socialisation in sport
points: Boys are given footballs and encouraged to be rough and competitive.
Girls are given dance classes and praised for being neat and graceful.
Comments such as 'throws like a girl' teach children that some physical skills belong to one sex.

notes.h: Social regulation of the body: definition and history
points: Social regulation of the body: the way society, through its norms, expectations, rules and media images, defines how bodies should look, move and behave.
This regulation determines which physical activity people feel is appropriate or available to them.
Past: women were historically excluded or restricted, for example barred from some events and clubs.
Past: women's competition distances were limited and dress rules restricted their participation.
Past: a belief that strenuous exercise harmed women's health discouraged women from taking part.
Women's boxing was first included in the Olympic Games in 2012, in London.

notes.h: Social regulation of the body today
points: Dress codes and kit expectations set out what women and men should wear to take part.
Muscular women, and men who take part in activities seen as feminine, are judged or criticised.
Unequal provision and pay for women's sport persist.
Appearance expectations continue to shape which activities people feel comfortable taking part in.

notes.h: Effects of social regulation on women and men
points: For women: girls are steered away from contact, power and strength sports and from visible muscle.
For women: women practise self-surveillance, constantly monitoring and judging their appearance.
For women: these pressures contribute to drop-out in adolescence.
For men: pressure to be strong, tough and competitive.
For men: avoidance of dance, gymnastics and synchronised swimming, which are seen as feminine.
For men: pressure to play through pain and injury.
For men: reluctance to show weakness or seek help.
Hegemonic masculinity: the dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a man in a society, treated as the norm against which men are measured.
It is a standard that individual men are measured against; it does not describe all men.
The concept was developed by the sociologist R. W. Connell.
Characteristics: physical strength, toughness, aggression, competitiveness, dominance, emotional restraint, risk-taking and heterosexuality.

notes.h: Hegemonic masculinity: impact on boys and girls
points: For boys: boys who fit the ideal gain high status in contact team sports.
For boys: boys who are less sporty or prefer aesthetic activities are excluded or ridiculed.
For boys: boys are encouraged to play through injury and violence.
For boys: boys who do not fit the ideal may drop out.
For girls: sport itself is defined as masculine, so girls who play are seen as less feminine.
For girls: women's sport is treated as second-rate.
Hegemonic femininity: the dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a woman in a society, treated as the norm against which women are measured.
It is a standard that individual women are measured against; it does not describe all women.
Characteristics: slimness, grace, attractiveness and an appearance focus, gentleness, passivity and non-aggression, caring and deference.

notes.h: Hegemonic femininity: impact on girls and boys
points: For girls: activities that are aggressive, muscular, sweaty or contact-based seem unfeminine, so girls avoid them or drop out.
For girls: an emphasis on appearance leads to self-consciousness about how they look while taking part.
For girls: they are channelled into aesthetic activities, such as dance or gymnastics.
For boys: activities linked to femininity, such as dance and gymnastics, are avoided for fear of ridicule.
Visible role models who break stereotypes, such as women playing rugby, boxing and Gaelic games, and men taking part in dance.
Equal provision and media coverage for women's and men's sport.
Mixed and choice-based PE, so boys and girls can choose activities without gender labels.
Coaches and teachers who challenge stereotyped comments as they happen.

keyTerms.definition: The lifelong process of learning the norms, values and behaviour that a society expects of its members.
The process of learning what is seen as appropriate for boys and men, and for girls and women.
The people and institutions, such as family, peers, school and media, that teach individuals a society's norms.
The way a society's norms, expectations, rules and media images define how bodies should look, move and behave.

The dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a man, treated as the norm against which men are measured.
The dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a woman, treated as the norm against which women are measured.

A fixed, oversimplified belief about what people of a particular group are like.

questions.prompt: Explain hegemonic femininity and hegemonic masculinity, and why each might impact on the participation of boys and girls.
questions.model: Hegemonic masculinity is the dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a man in a society, treated as the norm against which men are measured. Its characteristics include physical strength, toughness, aggression, competitiveness, dominance, emotional restraint, risk-taking and heterosexuality. Because contact team sports reward these traits, boys who fit gain status, while boys who are less sporty or prefer aesthetic activities may be excluded or ridiculed, and boys may be pushed to play through injury or drop out. Girls are also affected: sport itself is defined as masculine, so girls who play are seen as less feminine, and women's sport is treated as second-rate. Hegemonic femininity is the dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a woman, treated as the norm against which women are measured. Its characteristics include slimness, grace, attractiveness, an appearance focus, gentleness, passivity, non-aggression, caring and deference. Activities that are aggressive, muscular, sweaty or contact-based seem unfeminine, so girls avoid them or drop out, and an emphasis on appearance brings self-consciousness. Girls are channelled into aesthetic activities such as dance. Boys are affected too: activities linked to femininity, such as dance and gymnastics, are avoided for fear of ridicule, which narrows their choices.

questions.prompt: Discuss how social regulation of the body impacts on the participation levels of men and women in physical activity.
questions.model: Social regulation of the body is the way society, through its norms, expectations, rules and media images, defines how bodies should look, move and behave, which shapes the activities people feel are appropriate or available to them. Historically, women were excluded or restricted: they were barred from some events and clubs, competition distances were limited, dress rules applied, and a belief that strenuous exercise harmed women's health discouraged them from taking part. Women's boxing was first included in the Olympic Games in 2012, in London. Today, dress codes and kit expectations, judgement of muscular women or of men in feminine activities, and unequal provision and pay for women's sport continue to limit participation. For women, girls are steered away from contact, power and strength sports and from visible muscle, women practise self-surveillance of their appearance, and these pressures contribute to drop-out in adolescence. For men, the pressure to be strong, tough and competitive leads to avoidance of dance, gymnastics and synchronised swimming, pressure to play through pain and injury, and reluctance to show weakness or seek help. Women's participation is therefore narrowed by exclusion and appearance pressure, and men's by expectations of toughness.

questions.prompt: Explain hegemonic masculinity and give one way it can affect boys' participation in sport.
questions.model: Hegemonic masculinity is the dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a man in a society, treated as the norm against which men are measured. It is a standard rather than a description of every man, and it includes physical strength, toughness, aggression, competitiveness and emotional restraint. One way it affects boys' participation: boys who do not fit the ideal, for example those who are less sporty or prefer dance, may be excluded or ridiculed by peers, which may lead them to drop out of sport altogether.
